name: ngspice
why: A real SPICE circuit simulator lets you build and watch analog circuits run on your own machine.

brief.what_it_is: ngspice is an open source SPICE circuit simulator for electric and electronic circuits. You describe a circuit as a netlist, either as a text file or typed on the command line, and it simulates analog circuits built from transistors (JFET, bipolar, MOS), passive R, L, C elements, diodes, and transmission lines. It also simulates digital circuits, from single gates up to complex ones, and mixed analog/digital circuits. The output is one or more graphs of currents, voltages and other quantities, or a data file.
brief.why_it_exists: The site presents it as a free, SPICE-compatible simulator: newcomers are invited to try it, and professionals are promised robustness and flexibility. It can read PSPICE and LTSPICE model parameters and netlists, and HSPICE libraries from semiconductor foundry PDKs.
brief.how_it_works: The user writes a netlist of circuit elements and device models, and ngspice reads it, preprocesses it (compatibility, subcircuits, parameters), builds the circuit structure, sets up and solves the matrix, and runs the simulation. Device models come from its own collections, from semiconductor manufacturers, or from foundries. The homepage explicitly does not offer schematic entry; input is command line or file based, and third-party interfaces exist.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says ngspice builds on many operating systems: Windows source and binaries are on the SourceForge download page, and Linux distributions, Cygwin, FreeBSD and Homebrew for macOS also offer it. From the Homebrew metadata supplied with the request (not from the fetched pages): if you need the graphical plotting functions, install X11 with brew install --cask xquartz. No runtime or account is mentioned on the pages I fetched.
brief.standout: It is a long-running open source SPICE that accepts PSPICE, LTSPICE and HSPICE model files, including foundry PDK libraries, so it can run circuits written for commercial tools. Its digital and mixed-signal event-driven simulation is also built in, which is less common in free SPICE tools.
brief.status: maintained, on indirect evidence. The homepage cites FOSDEM talks through 2025, the docs page links a current user manual (version 47) plus an 'updated' manual that tracks git sources, and it says the manual is under continuous development. I did not find a release date or last-commit date on these pages.
brief.caveats: No schematic entry; you write netlists or use third-party front ends. Plotting needs X11 (XQuartz on macOS) per the Homebrew note. The site says the manual is a work in progress that may change without notice, and it has known minor bugs. The internals documents are Excel or Word files. Text is under the GNU Free Documentation License.
